rationale: The entry builds a coherent obedience theme, especially from John 4:34, Luke 8:21, and Hebrews 5:14, but it does not establish that this is the uniform symbolic referent of “meat.” The strongest contextual reading distinguishes several food metaphors: John 4 calls completing the Father’s work Jesus’ food; John 6 calls Christ’s flesh true food; Hebrews 5 and 1 Corinthians 3 use solid food for teaching suited to mature hearers. Most decisively, Hebrews 5:14 distinguishes the food from the people qualified to receive it: strong meat belongs to those whose senses have been exercised by use. The book turns a characteristic of mature eaters into the definition of the food itself. Its claim that milk and meat are the same word in two states also fits the pedagogical contrasts less naturally than the explicit distinction between elementary instruction and teaching for the mature.
book_core_identification: Meat symbolizes the word of God brought to completion through obedience, rather than advanced teaching as distinct content.
book_secondary_elaborations: Milk is the word merely received.
Milk and meat are the same word in different states.
Carrying the word through to complete obedience exercises the senses to discern.
unsupported_glossary_assertions: That “meat” generally denotes the word obeyed to completeness rather than, contextually, food, Christ’s flesh, or teaching suited to maturity.
That milk and meat are necessarily the same word in two states rather than contrasting levels or forms of instruction.
That Hebrews 5:14 defines meat as the obedient exercise of discernment, rather than describing the practiced maturity of those to whom strong meat belongs.
chapter_only_objections: The appeal to churning milk into butter in Proverbs 30:33 does not establish a biblical milk-to-meat transformation.
The Hebrew milk/fat consonantal observation and the proposed combined reading of Ezekiel 34 are text-critical elaborations not needed by the glossary entry.
The bread–flesh–meat and basar/good-tidings wordplay in the John 6 argument requires several typological and lexical steps not stated by the passage.
The claim that biblical symbols must hold one uniform meaning across all occurrences is difficult to reconcile with the plainly contextual uses of food language.
The chapter’s broader claim that the gospel becomes meat only when obeyed is not asserted in the glossary entry.
strongest_counter_interpretation: “Meat” is not a single uniform technical symbol. In the milk/meat passages it means substantial teaching appropriate to mature believers, while John 4 uses food as a separate metaphor for accomplishing God’s will and John 6 identifies Christ’s flesh as true food. Practiced obedience and discernment qualify a person to receive solid teaching but are not the referent of the food itself.
counter_core_identification: In the controlling milk-versus-meat passages, meat is substantial spiritual instruction suited to mature believers; obedience and practiced discernment describe the mature recipient rather than define the instruction.
material_core_denial: The scriptural evidence does not justify equating meat itself with the word obeyed to completion; it more directly distinguishes strong food from the maturity acquired through use that enables a person to receive it.
counter_case: Hebrews 5:12-14 grammatically separates “strong meat” from those who, “by reason of use,” have exercised senses; practice characterizes the eaters, while meat is what belongs to them.

Hebrews 5:12 and 6:1-2 contrast elementary principles that must be taught again with progress toward perfection, naturally indicating levels of instruction rather than one teaching transformed by obedience.
In 1 Corinthians 2:6–3:2, Paul contrasts wisdom spoken among the mature with milk given to carnal infants, again making hearer maturity govern the level of teaching supplied.
John 4:34 explicitly supports doing and finishing God’s will as nourishment, but its first-person expression—“My meat”—does not require that every pedagogical use of meat carry that definition.
John 6:55 explicitly calls Christ’s flesh meat, showing that food imagery can have a distinct christological referent rather than the glossary’s single proposed definition.
The KJV term “meat” commonly means food and represents contextual food metaphors; treating the shared English label as a uniform symbolic key risks conflating distinct passages.
book_explanatory_advantages: John 4:34 directly associates Jesus’ meat with doing the Sender’s will and finishing His work.
Matthew 12:50 and Luke 8:21 plausibly connect doing the Father’s will with hearing and doing God’s word.
Hebrews 5:14 does associate strong meat with practiced use and exercised discernment.
The entry offers an integrated ethical account of why maturity and discernment accompany meat.
counter_explanatory_advantages: It preserves the grammatical distinction in Hebrews between solid food and the practiced maturity of its recipients.
It accounts naturally for the pedagogical context of Hebrews 5–6 and 1 Corinthians 2–3.
It allows John 4 and John 6 to retain their explicit, context-specific referents without forcing them into one technical definition.
It requires fewer typological and lexical bridges than identifying Christ’s flesh, mature teaching, and completed obedience as one referent.
It accommodates the ordinary KJV sense of “meat” as food and the resulting diversity of food metaphors.
evidence_book_core_cannot_explain: Hebrews 5:14 says strong meat “belongeth to” people whose senses have already been exercised by use; identifying the meat with that exercise collapses the passage’s distinction between the food and the qualification of its recipients.
John 6:55 directly predicates meat of Christ’s flesh. The exact glossary core cannot absorb that identification without importing the chapter’s additional Word-made-flesh typology.

The elementary-principles versus maturity structure of Hebrews 5:12–6:2 identifies a difference in instructional level that the assertion “the same word” does not preserve without reinterpreting the passage’s explicit pedagogical contrast.
unresolved_objections: John 4:34 remains unusually direct evidence for the book’s obedience-centered meaning in that particular context.
Luke 8:21 and Matthew 12:50 provide a legitimate connection between God’s will and hearing and doing God’s word.
The boundary between mature teaching and teaching appropriated through obedient practice may be less sharp pastorally than it is lexically.
